calc.draft: Draft: these rules are still being checked by a lawyer.
calc.awl: The fixed shares added up to more than the whole estate, so each share was reduced in the same proportion (called awl).
calc.disclaimer: This is a plain-language guide, not legal advice. A will, debts, property already given away and special family situations can change the shares. Have a lawyer or court confirm the final division.

explain.title: A lawyer needs to work this out
explain.intro: Under this law the shares depend on specific facts about the family and the property, so we do not guess.

r.spouseFixed: The surviving spouse receives {{frac}} of the estate.
r.childrenRest: The children share the rest equally.
r.childrenAll: With no surviving spouse, the children share the whole estate equally.
r.spouseAll: With no children and no other relatives, the spouse receives everything.
r.husbandNoChild: One-half, because there are no children.
r.wifeNoChild: One-quarter (shared equally if there is more than one wife), because there are no children.
r.wifeChild: One-eighth (shared equally if there is more than one wife), because there are children.
r.motherNoChild: One-third, because there are no children.
r.motherUmar: One-third of what remains after the spouse's share, because only the spouse and both parents survive.
r.fatherChild: One-sixth, because there is a son.
r.fatherDaughters: One-sixth, plus whatever remains after the fixed shares.
r.fatherResidue: Everything that remains after the other shares.
r.daughterHalf: One-half, because she is the only daughter and there are no sons.
r.daughtersTwoThirds: Two-thirds shared equally among the daughters, because there are no sons.
r.sonsDaughters: They share what remains. Each son receives twice a daughter's share.

lk-general.title: General law
lk-general.desc: Applies to most people who are not under Kandyan, Thesawalamai or Muslim law.

lk-kandyan.title: Kandyan law
lk-kandyan.desc: Usually for Sinhalese families with Kandyan roots (not only religion).
points: Whether the property is ancestral (paraveni) or acquired matters.
Whether a daughter's marriage was binna (staying in the family home) or diga (moving to her husband's home) can change her rights.
A widow may get a life interest in some property rather than full ownership.
Courts apply these rules case by case, so get a lawyer's opinion.

lk-thesawalamai.title: Thesawalamai law
lk-thesawalamai.desc: Usually for Tamil families of Jaffna origin.
points: Property acquired during the marriage (thediathetam) is treated differently from inherited property.
The share of the surviving spouse depends on the kind of property.
Property that came from the mother's side and from the father's side may pass differently.
How to classify a property is often disputed, so a lawyer is essential.

lk-muslim.title: Muslim law
lk-muslim.desc: For Muslims. Sunni rules are used here.

lk-unsure.title: Not sure
lk-unsure.desc: We will show you what to ask.
points: Is the family Muslim? Then Muslim law applies.
Is the family of Jaffna Tamil background? Then Thesawalamai usually applies.
Is the family Sinhalese with Kandyan roots? Then Kandyan law may apply.
If none of these fit, the general law usually applies. Confirm with a lawyer.

pk-shia.title: Muslim (Shia)
pk-shia.desc: Shia rules differ from Sunni rules, so a lawyer is needed.
points: In Shia law the shares of some relatives, for example in a family with only daughters, differ from the Sunni rules.
So the Sunni calculation cannot be applied to a Shia family.
Speak to a scholar or lawyer who knows the Jafari school.

pk-other.title: Hindu, Sikh, Parsi or other
pk-other.desc: These communities usually follow their own personal law or custom.
points: Hindus, Sikhs and some other communities generally follow their own personal law or custom.
Parsis have separate provisions in the Succession Act, 1925.
For exact shares, speak to a lawyer who knows your community's law.

pk-unsure.title: Not sure
pk-unsure.desc: We will show you what to ask.
points: Muslim family: choose Sunni or Shia as applies.
Christian family: the Succession Act, 1925 applies.
Other communities: ask a lawyer about their personal law.
If you are not sure, confirm with a lawyer.
